items.prompt: What actually makes air rush into the lungs when you breathe in?

options.label: The nose and throat push air down using tiny muscles
options.feedback: Nothing in the nose or throat forces air downward; air moves because of a pressure difference created much further down, around the lungs themselves.

options.label: The lungs actively suck air in by squeezing themselves
options.feedback: Lung tissue has no muscle of its own to squeeze or suck with; it can only follow the space around it as that space changes.

options.label: Air is pulled in by the beating of the heart nearby
options.feedback: The heart's beat moves blood, not air, and has no direct effect on pulling air into the lungs.

options.label: The chest cavity expands, dropping the pressure inside it below the pressure outside
options.feedback: Once the space around the lungs grows larger, the air pressure inside it falls below the pressure outside, and outside air pushes in to even it out.

items.ok_line: Make more room, and outside air rushes in to fill it.
items.ko_line: The lungs themselves have no muscle to squeeze with — the movement starts somewhere else.
items.exp_text: Air, like any gas, flows from an area of higher pressure toward an area of lower pressure until the two match. When the space enclosing the lungs is made larger, the air already inside it spreads out and its pressure drops below that of the air outside the body. Outside air then flows in through the nose and airway simply to equalise that pressure, filling the lungs as it goes.

items.prompt: What does the diaphragm actually do when you breathe in?

options.label: It contracts and flattens downward, enlarging the chest cavity
options.feedback: As the diaphragm contracts it pulls flatter and moves down, giving the chest cavity above it more room than it had a moment before.

options.label: It pumps air directly into the windpipe
options.feedback: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle below the lungs, not a pump connected to the windpipe; it changes the space the lungs sit in rather than moving air itself.

options.label: It filters dust out of the incoming air
options.feedback: Filtering incoming air is handled higher up, in the nose and airway lining; the diaphragm's job is entirely about changing the shape of the chest cavity.

options.label: It relaxes and rises to squeeze air out of the lungs
options.feedback: That describes what the diaphragm does when breathing out, the opposite of what happens on a breath in.

items.ok_title: Down and flatter, more room above
items.ok_line: A dome that flattens to make space, not a pump that pushes air.
items.ko_line: The diaphragm changes the shape of the space the lungs sit in — it does not touch the air directly.
items.exp_title: A dome that flattens for room
items.exp_text: At rest, the diaphragm sits curved upward like a dome underneath the lungs. Breathing in starts when this sheet of muscle contracts, pulling itself flatter and shifting downward, and that flattening enlarges the cavity the lungs sit inside. With more room to expand into, the lungs stretch outward and air is drawn in behind them to fill the new space.

items.prompt: Why do the airways inside the lungs keep branching into smaller and smaller tubes rather than opening straight into one wide space?

options.label: Branching keeps different smells separated as air passes through
options.feedback: Detecting smell happens up in the nose, long before air reaches the branching airways of the lungs; separating scents plays no part in why the tubes divide.

options.label: Branching lets the lungs fold up smaller when not in use
options.feedback: The lungs do not fold away between breaths; the branching structure stays filled with air and expanded even at rest, so this is not what the branching achieves.

options.label: Branching slows the air down so it has time to warm up
options.feedback: Warming incoming air happens mostly in the nose and upper airway before it reaches the branching tubes deep in the lungs; that is not the reason for the branching itself.

options.label: Repeated branching multiplies the surface area available for gas exchange
options.feedback: Splitting one wide passage into millions of narrow branching tubes, each ending in its own tiny sac, packs vastly more exchange surface into the same overall space.

items.ok_line: One wide tube ending in one wide sac would offer far less surface than millions of narrow branches ending in millions of tiny ones.
items.ko_line: Think about what gas exchange actually needs more of, and how splitting a space into many small ones changes that.
items.exp_title: Splitting a space to grow its surface
items.exp_text: Oxygen and carbon dioxide can only cross between air and blood at a surface where the two meet, so how much surface is available limits how much gas can be exchanged at once. A single large chamber has comparatively little surface for its volume, while the same volume divided into countless small branching tubes, each ending in a tiny air sac, has vastly more surface packed into it. The lungs branch again and again because splitting the space this way is what lets a modest volume of air do the work of a much larger one.

items.prompt: What actually happens inside one of the tiny air sacs at the end of the lungs' airways?

options.label: Oxygen crosses into the blood while carbon dioxide crosses out, through a very thin wall
options.feedback: The sac's wall is thin enough, and pressed close enough against a blood vessel, that gas moves straight across it in both directions.

options.label: Air is stored there until the next breath is needed
options.feedback: These sacs are not storage spaces; their whole surface is dedicated to exchanging gas with the blood, not holding air in reserve.

options.label: Dust and germs are trapped and dissolved there
options.feedback: Trapping incoming particles is handled higher up, by mucus lining the airway walls before air ever reaches these delicate sacs.

options.label: Sound vibrations are produced there for speaking
options.feedback: Sound for speech is produced further up the airway, not down in these small sacs, whose whole job is exchanging gas with the blood.

items.ok_title: A crossing point, both ways at once
items.ok_line: Oxygen goes one way across the wall, carbon dioxide goes the other.
items.ko_line: Every one of these tiny sacs is wrapped by a blood vessel — ask what would need to cross between the two.
items.exp_title: A wall thin enough to cross
items.exp_text: Each tiny air sac is wrapped almost entirely by a fine blood vessel, and the wall separating the air inside the sac from the blood inside that vessel is only a single thin layer of cells. Oxygen dissolved in the fresh air passes straight through that thin wall into the blood, while carbon dioxide carried by the blood passes the other way, out into the air to be breathed away. Both gases move simply because each is more concentrated on one side of the wall than the other.

items.prompt: Where does the carbon dioxide in the breath you exhale actually come from?

options.label: It is produced by the airway lining as air passes through it
options.feedback: The tissue lining the airway does not manufacture carbon dioxide as air brushes past it; the gas is delivered there from the bloodstream instead.

options.label: It is left over from the oxygen you breathed in, unused by the lungs
options.feedback: The carbon dioxide breathed out is not leftover inhaled oxygen; it is a separate gas produced elsewhere in the body and delivered to the lungs by the blood.

options.label: It is a waste product carried to the lungs by blood from cells all over the body
options.feedback: Cells throughout the body release carbon dioxide as they burn fuel for energy, and blood carries it back to the lungs to be breathed out.

options.label: It is absorbed from the air of the room while you were breathing it in
options.feedback: Room air contains only a small trace of carbon dioxide, far less than what actually leaves the body in each breath, so it cannot be the source of what is exhaled.

items.ok_line: Every cell in the body makes this waste gas, and the blood ferries it back to be breathed out.
items.ko_line: Ask what is happening in cells far from the lungs, long before that air is ever exhaled.
items.exp_title: A waste gas delivered from far away
items.exp_text: Cells throughout the body release energy from their fuel by combining it with oxygen, and carbon dioxide is the waste left over from that process, produced continuously in tissue everywhere, not just near the lungs. Blood picks this gas up as it passes through those tissues and carries it all the way back to the lungs. Once there, it crosses out of the blood and into the air sacs, ready to leave the body on the next breath out.

items.prompt: Why does the windpipe stay open even when the tube behind it, the esophagus, collapses flat between swallows?

options.label: Air pressure alone is enough to keep any tube inflated
options.feedback: Air pressure does not automatically hold a soft tube open; without the cartilage rings, the windpipe would collapse the same way the esophagus does.

options.label: The windpipe is reinforced with rings of stiff cartilage
options.feedback: A series of stiff cartilage rings runs along the windpipe, holding it open as a rigid tube even when nothing is passing through it.

options.label: The windpipe is lined with muscle strong enough to hold its shape
options.feedback: Muscle in the windpipe's wall is soft tissue that would sag without support; what actually keeps the tube's shape is the stiff cartilage reinforcing it.

options.label: The windpipe is shorter, so it has less tube to collapse
options.feedback: Length is not the reason one tube stays open and the other does not; it comes down to what is built into each tube's wall.

items.ok_title: A tube with a built-in frame
items.ok_line: Rings of cartilage hold the shape open, air pressure or not.
items.ko_line: The esophagus is a soft tube with nothing rigid in its wall; the windpipe has something extra.
items.exp_title: A tube with its own scaffolding
items.exp_text: The esophagus only ever needs to open when food is being swallowed through it, so its soft muscular wall stays collapsed flat the rest of the time. The windpipe, by contrast, has to stay open at every moment so air can pass in either direction, and a series of curved cartilage rings runs along its length to hold that shape rigidly. Squeeze either tube gently from outside, and the one reinforced with cartilage keeps its shape while the other flattens.

items.prompt: Why can you not hold your breath indefinitely, no matter how hard you try?

options.label: The lungs run out of oxygen and simply stop responding
options.feedback: Oxygen levels in the blood generally have not dropped by very much by the time the urge to breathe becomes overwhelming; the true trigger is a different gas building up.

options.label: Carbon dioxide builds up in the blood and triggers an overwhelming urge to breathe
options.feedback: It is rising carbon dioxide, sensed by the body, that drives the mounting discomfort of holding a breath, not the oxygen level running low.

options.label: The diaphragm becomes physically too tired to stay still
options.feedback: The diaphragm can hold a position for a while without tiring in that way; the urge to breathe again comes from a chemical signal, not from muscle fatigue.

options.label: The brain forgets that breathing has been paused
options.feedback: Far from forgetting, the brain is actively monitoring the blood the whole time and grows increasingly insistent as one particular gas accumulates.

items.ok_title: A gas building up, not one running out
items.ok_line: It is rising carbon dioxide that forces the next breath, not falling oxygen.
items.ko_line: The discomfort of holding a breath arrives well before oxygen has actually run low.
items.exp_title: The trigger is a gas rising, not falling
items.exp_text: While a breath is held, the body keeps producing carbon dioxide as usual, but with no fresh breath to carry it away, the gas steadily builds up in the blood. Sensors that monitor the blood detect that rising level and send an increasingly urgent signal telling the diaphragm to contract again. The overwhelming urge to breathe that eventually forces a held breath to end is driven by that build-up, not by the body running short of oxygen.

items.prompt: Why does breathing continue steadily even while you are asleep or thinking about something else entirely?

options.label: A part of the brain sets the rhythm automatically, without needing conscious control
options.feedback: A region of the brain generates a steady, repeating signal to the breathing muscles on its own, running whether or not any attention is being paid to it.

options.label: The lungs contract on their own without any signal at all
options.feedback: Lung tissue has no muscle of its own to contract with; the rhythm still comes from a signal sent to the diaphragm and chest muscles, even if no one is paying attention to it.

options.label: The heart's beat also triggers each breath alongside it
options.feedback: Breathing and heartbeat are controlled by separate systems running on their own independent rhythms, not one triggering the other.

options.label: Breathing pauses completely during sleep and restarts on waking
options.feedback: Breathing does not stop during ordinary sleep; the same automatic rhythm keeps running throughout, adjusting itself as needed without ever fully halting.

items.ok_line: A region of the brain keeps the rhythm running whether or not anyone is thinking about it.
items.ko_line: Breathing has to keep working during sleep, so the signal driving it cannot depend on conscious attention.
items.exp_title: A rhythm that runs without asking
items.exp_text: A region at the base of the brain generates a steady, repeating signal that travels down to the diaphragm and the muscles of the chest, telling them when to contract and when to relax. This rhythm runs continuously in the background, adjusted moment to moment by chemical signals from the blood rather than by conscious thought. Breathing can be deliberately sped up, slowed down, or held for a while, but as soon as attention moves elsewhere, this automatic rhythm simply takes back over.

items.prompt: What is actually happening inside the chest during a hiccup?

options.label: The stomach squeezes air back up through the windpipe
options.feedback: A hiccup does not begin in the stomach pushing air upward; it begins with a sudden contraction of the diaphragm below the lungs.

options.label: The diaphragm suddenly contracts, and the airway snaps shut right after
options.feedback: A hiccup starts with a sudden, involuntary jerk of the diaphragm pulling air in, immediately followed by a small structure at the top of the airway snapping shut, which produces the characteristic sound.

options.label: The lungs briefly stop working and restart with a jolt
options.feedback: The lungs themselves do not switch off during a hiccup; it is a sudden, isolated spasm of the diaphragm that triggers the whole event.

options.label: Cold air passing over the vocal cords makes them vibrate suddenly
options.feedback: A hiccup is not caused by air temperature acting on the voice; it is triggered by a sudden, involuntary contraction of the diaphragm.

items.ok_line: The diaphragm jerks, air rushes in, and the airway slams shut right behind it.
items.ko_line: A hiccup starts below the lungs, with a muscle jerking suddenly out of its usual rhythm.
items.exp_text: A hiccup begins when the diaphragm contracts suddenly and out of its usual smooth rhythm, pulling a quick, involuntary gulp of air inward. Almost instantly afterward, a small flap-like structure at the top of the windpipe snaps shut in response, cutting that inward rush of air off abruptly. The sharp sound of a hiccup is produced at the exact moment the airway closes against that sudden, misfired breath.

items.prompt: Why do the lungs never fully empty of air, even after breathing all the way out?

options.label: The windpipe is too narrow to let all the air pass through
options.feedback: The windpipe is wide enough to let air move freely in either direction; a narrow passage is not what leaves air behind in the lungs.

options.label: The body needs the leftover air as a store of extra oxygen
options.feedback: The air left behind after breathing out is largely used up rather than fresh, so it works poorly as an oxygen reserve; that is not why it stays behind.

options.label: The branching tubes and air sacs would collapse and stick shut if fully emptied
options.feedback: Leaving a cushion of air behind keeps the delicate, moist walls of the air sacs from collapsing flat against each other and sticking together.

options.label: The diaphragm cannot rise high enough to push every bit of air out
options.feedback: The diaphragm rises a good deal on a full breath out, but the leftover air is left behind on purpose, to protect the structure of the lungs, not because the diaphragm falls short.

items.ok_line: Emptying completely would let the delicate air sacs collapse against themselves.
items.ko_line: Think about what would happen to the walls of the tiniest air sacs if every last breath of air left them.
items.exp_text: The walls of the tiny air sacs deep in the lungs are thin, moist and delicate, built that way so gas can cross them easily. If every trace of air were pushed out, those moist walls would tend to stick to each other and collapse, making the next breath in far harder than it needs to be. A small volume of air stays behind after every breath out, propping the sacs open and keeping the lungs ready for the next breath without having to reinflate from nothing.
